title: The church sings (Colossians 3:16)
hook: the first Christians sang psalms, hymns and spiritual songs

segments.voice: Yesterday: hospitality, love of the stranger, and Abraham running to three guests in the heat. Your line was strangers might be angels. Who did you offer a drink to? Day one hundred thirty-five.

Think of the last time a room full of people sang together. A birthday, a stadium, a funeral where nobody could quite hold the note. Something happens when voices go up at once that doesn't happen when one person talks. You may remember Paul and Silas from day eighty-four, singing in the stocks at Philippi while the prisoners listened. That night wasn't a one-off. Wherever the first Christians turn up, there's a song close by. A Roman official heard about it. A letter from Paul tells a small church what kind of songs to use. And the Gospels put a song at the very start, on the night before the cross. Christians have kept it up in every century since, in cathedrals, in basements, in fields: when they gather, they sing. Today, the church sings.
screen: `A ROOM FULL OF VOICES.` → `PAUL AND SILAS WEREN'T A ONE-OFF.` → `WHEN THEY GATHER, THEY SING.`

segments.voice: The church sang from the very first night. The Gospel of Mark says that after the last supper, before they walked out to the Mount of Olives, Jesus and his friends sang: "And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives." Many scholars think it was psalms that Jews sang at Passover, the ones still sung at the Passover table today. So the church's first song was a Jewish song. Then Paul, writing to the Christians in Colossae, describes what their gatherings sounded like. In the King James Bible: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." Psalms, hymns, spiritual songs. Nobody knows exactly where one ends and the next begins. Psalms likely means the old songs of Israel. Hymns, songs of praise. Spiritual songs might be something newer, even made up in the moment. Notice who's teaching whom: one another. Singing was how they taught. A tune carries words into memory in a way a lecture can't. And outsiders noticed. Around the year 112, a Roman governor named Pliny wrote to the emperor about these odd people called Christians. He reported that they met before dawn on a fixed day and sang a hymn to Christ, as to a god. A Roman official, not a friend, is one of our earliest witnesses that they sang. Today's line, who sings prays twice, is often credited to Saint Augustine. Scholars can't find those exact words in his writings. But he did write about weeping when he heard the church sing. The idea stuck because so many people recognize it: when you sing a prayer, your breath and your body pray it too.
screen: `THEY SANG AN HYMN, AND WENT OUT.` · `PSALMS, HYMNS, SPIRITUAL SONGS.` · `SINGING WAS HOW THEY TAUGHT.` · `A ROMAN HEARD THEM BEFORE DAWN.` · then, large: `WHO SINGS PRAYS TWICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. You don't need a good voice. You barely need a voice at all. Think of one line of a hymn or church song you know, any one. Amazing grace. Holy, holy, holy. Jesus loves me. If none come to mind, hum a tune you remember from a wedding or a funeral. Breathe in, and sing or hum that one line, softly, once. Then again, slower. Notice where the sound sits in your chest. If you pray, let the line be your prayer. If you don't, just notice what a song does to your breath. The bell holds the time.
Spiritual songs, Paul's third kind of church music, maybe newer, even made up in the moment, alongside psalms and hymns.
Your line: who sings prays twice. Today, sing or hum one line of a hymn, in the shower, in the car, under your breath. Day one hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Nearly every Christian church sings when it gathers: Orthodox and many Catholic services chant much of the liturgy, and Protestant congregations sing hymns and worship songs together, often with an organ, piano or band.

trapdoor: what you thought: church music is something added on to church.
what it means: from the first night, singing was how Christians prayed, remembered and taught one another.
what a scholar hears: one of the earliest outside witnesses is Pliny's letter to Trajan, around 112: Christians sang a hymn to Christ, as to a god, before dawn.

notes: Mark 14:26: the hymn is often identified with the Hallel (Psalms 113–118), sung at Passover; stated as 'many scholars think'. Confirm.
Pliny, Letters 10.96 (c. 111–113): 'carmen Christo quasi deo dicere'. Carmen may mean a chant or set form of words rather than a song; script says 'sang a hymn'. Confirm.
'Who sings prays twice' (qui cantat bis orat): attributed to Augustine but not found verbatim in his works; stated plainly. Confirm.
Augustine weeping at the church's hymns: Confessions 9.6.14. Confirm reference.
Distinctions among psalms, hymns and spiritual songs: presented as uncertain. Confirm.
Original: Greek of Col 3:16 in the dative; confirm spelling and accents, and the transliteration (modern-ish pronunciation used).

Audit (second sample): the hook retold day 84's scene (Paul and Silas singing at midnight in the stocks) almost word for word, and the myth item ('sang only after they were freed') and the fork repeated day 84's. The hook now opens on a room singing together and names day 84 as a callback; the myth now asks about the Passover hymn and the fork about Pliny's report, both taught today.
